definition: A topology on a set X is a collection T of subsets of X (called open sets) satisfying: (1) the empty set and X are in T, (2) any union of sets in T is in T, (3) any finite intersection of sets in T is in T. The pair (X, T) is a topological space. Topology studies properties preserved under continuous deformations (homeomorphisms).

contrasts.differential: A metric space has a distance function; a topological space has only the abstract notion of open sets. Every metric induces a topology but not every topology comes from a metric

definition: A member of the topology T on a topological space (X, T). In a metric space, a set U is open if for every point x in U there exists epsilon > 0 such that the open ball B(x, epsilon) is contained in U. Open sets are the primitive undefined objects of general topology — the topology is defined by specifying which sets are open.

contrasts.differential: A set is closed iff its complement is open. A set can be both open and closed (clopen), or neither

definition: A subset A of a topological space X whose complement X \ A is open. Equivalently, a set that contains all its limit points. The closure of a set A is the smallest closed set containing A. Closed sets are closed under finite union and arbitrary intersection.

contrasts.differential: Open sets are closed under arbitrary union and finite intersection; closed sets are closed under arbitrary intersection and finite union

definition: A neighborhood of a point x in a topological space X is any open set U containing x. More generally, a set N is a neighborhood of x if there exists an open set U with x in U and U contained in N. The neighborhood system of a point can be used as an alternative axiomatization of topology.

contrasts.differential: Every open set containing x is a neighborhood; a neighborhood need not be open (it only needs to contain an open set around x)

definition: A function f: X -> Y between topological spaces is continuous if for every open set V in Y, the preimage f^{-1}(V) is open in X. Equivalently: f is continuous at a point x if for every neighborhood V of f(x), there exists a neighborhood U of x such that f(U) is contained in V. Continuity is the fundamental morphism concept in topology.

contrasts.differential: A continuous function need not be invertible; a homeomorphism is a bijective continuous function with continuous inverse
Continuity requires preimages of open sets to be open; an open map requires images of open sets to be open. Neither implies the other

definition: A bijective continuous function f: X -> Y between topological spaces whose inverse f^{-1} is also continuous. Equivalently, a bijection such that U is open in X iff f(U) is open in Y. Homeomorphism is the equivalence relation of topology — two spaces are 'topologically the same' if they are homeomorphic. Topological properties are those preserved by homeomorphisms.

contrasts.differential: Homeomorphism preserves all topological properties; homotopy equivalence is weaker — it preserves algebraic invariants (fundamental group, homology) but not all topological properties (e.g., dimension)
Isometry preserves distances (metric property); homeomorphism only preserves topology (open sets)

definition: A topological space X is connected if it cannot be written as the union of two disjoint non-empty open sets. Equivalently, the only subsets of X that are both open and closed are the empty set and X itself. The continuous image of a connected space is connected. Connected components partition any space into maximal connected subspaces.

contrasts.differential: Path-connected implies connected but not conversely. Path-connected means any two points can be joined by a continuous path
A disconnected space has a separation: a partition into two non-empty open sets

definition: A topological space X is path-connected if for every pair of points x, y in X, there exists a continuous function (path) p: [0,1] -> X with p(0) = x and p(1) = y. Path-connectedness implies connectedness but not conversely. For locally path-connected spaces (including manifolds and CW complexes), the two notions coincide.

contrasts.differential: Connected only requires no separation into disjoint open sets; path-connected requires explicit paths between any two points
Simply connected means path-connected AND every loop is contractible to a point (trivial fundamental group)

definition: A topological space X is compact if every open cover of X has a finite subcover. In metric spaces, compactness is equivalent to being closed and bounded (Heine-Borel theorem for R^n), and also equivalent to sequential compactness (every sequence has a convergent subsequence). Compactness is one of the most important properties in topology.

contrasts.differential: In R^n, compact = closed + bounded. In general metric spaces, compact implies closed and bounded but not conversely. In non-metrizable spaces, 'bounded' may not even be defined
In metric spaces, compact = sequentially compact. In general topological spaces, they differ

definition: The fundamental group pi_1(X, x_0) of a topological space X with basepoint x_0 is the group of homotopy classes of loops based at x_0, with concatenation as the group operation. It is a topological invariant: homeomorphic spaces have isomorphic fundamental groups. pi_1(S^1) = Z, pi_1(S^n) = 0 for n >= 2. The fundamental group detects 1-dimensional 'holes' in the space.

contrasts.differential: The fundamental group is a homotopy invariant defined via loops; homology groups are defined via chains and boundaries. pi_1 is generally non-abelian; H_1 is always abelian (H_1 is the abelianization of pi_1)
pi_1 uses loops (maps of S^1); pi_n uses maps of S^n. Higher homotopy groups are always abelian

definition: Homology assigns a sequence of abelian groups H_n(X) to a topological space X, measuring its n-dimensional 'holes'. H_0 counts connected components, H_1 counts independent loops, H_2 counts enclosed cavities. Formally, H_n = ker(d_n)/im(d_{n+1}) where d is the boundary operator of a chain complex. Homology is a homotopy invariant and satisfies the Eilenberg-Steenrod axioms.

contrasts.differential: Homology uses chains (formal sums of simplices); cohomology uses cochains (functions on chains). Cohomology has a natural ring structure (cup product) that homology lacks
Homology is abelian and computable; homotopy groups are generally non-abelian and harder to compute. Homology detects some but not all homotopy-theoretic information

definition: Cohomology assigns a sequence of abelian groups H^n(X) to a space X, dual to homology. Formally, apply Hom(-, G) to the chain complex to get a cochain complex, whose cohomology is H^n(X; G). Cohomology has a ring structure via the cup product, making it strictly richer than homology. De Rham cohomology uses differential forms.

contrasts.differential: Homology is covariant (pushforward); cohomology is contravariant (pullback). Cohomology has a ring structure (cup product); homology does not
Singular cohomology is purely algebraic-topological; de Rham cohomology uses smooth differential forms on manifolds. They agree for smooth manifolds by de Rham's theorem

definition: The n-th Betti number b_n(X) is the rank of the n-th homology group H_n(X; Z) modulo torsion, equivalently the dimension of H_n(X; Q) or H_n(X; R). b_0 = number of connected components, b_1 = number of independent loops (first Betti number = cycle rank for graphs), b_2 = number of enclosed cavities. The Euler characteristic chi = sum of (-1)^n * b_n.

contrasts.differential: Betti numbers give detailed information about each dimension; the Euler characteristic is a single number that alternately sums/subtracts Betti numbers
Betti numbers capture the free part of homology; torsion coefficients capture the finite cyclic group factors

definition: A topological invariant defined as chi(X) = sum_{n>=0} (-1)^n * b_n where b_n are Betti numbers. For a finite simplicial complex: chi = V - E + F - ... (alternating sum of simplex counts). For surfaces: chi = 2 - 2g (g = genus). The Euler characteristic is multiplicative under products and additive under disjoint unions.

contrasts.differential: Euler characteristic is a single integer; Betti numbers are a sequence. The Euler characteristic loses information by alternating-summing the Betti numbers
For orientable surfaces, chi = 2 - 2g. Genus g counts handles; chi is a more general invariant defined for any topological space

definition: A topological manifold is a second-countable Hausdorff space in which every point has a neighborhood homeomorphic to R^n (or equivalently to an open subset of R^n). The dimension n is a topological invariant. Manifolds are the fundamental objects of differential geometry and topology — locally they look like Euclidean space but can have complex global topology.

contrasts.differential: Manifolds are locally Euclidean; CW complexes are built inductively by attaching cells. Every manifold is a CW complex but not conversely
In algebraic geometry, varieties are defined by polynomial equations; manifolds are defined by local Euclidean structure. Smooth varieties are manifolds

definition: An abstract simplicial complex K on a vertex set V is a collection of finite subsets (simplices) of V such that: (1) every single vertex {v} is in K, (2) every subset of a simplex in K is also in K. A k-simplex has k+1 vertices. The geometric realization |K| gives a topological space. Simplicial complexes are the combinatorial foundation of algebraic topology.

contrasts.differential: Simplicial complexes are built from simplices with combinatorial gluing rules; CW complexes use arbitrary cells with continuous attaching maps. CW complexes are more flexible
A graph is a 1-dimensional simplicial complex (vertices and edges only). Simplicial complexes extend to arbitrary dimension with triangles, tetrahedra, etc.

definition: A CW complex is a topological space built inductively by starting with a discrete set of 0-cells (points) and attaching n-cells (copies of the n-disk D^n) via continuous maps from their boundary spheres S^{n-1}. The 'C' stands for closure-finite, the 'W' for weak topology. CW complexes are the standard class of spaces in algebraic topology — they are general enough to model any homotopy type yet structured enough for computation.

contrasts.differential: CW complexes attach cells via continuous maps; simplicial complexes use combinatorial face relations. CW complexes can represent spaces with fewer cells
Every manifold admits a CW structure but not every CW complex is a manifold (cells may not patch together to form locally Euclidean neighborhoods)

definition: A k-simplex is the convex hull of k+1 affinely independent points in R^n: sigma = {sum t_i v_i : t_i >= 0, sum t_i = 1}. A 0-simplex is a point, 1-simplex is an edge, 2-simplex is a triangle, 3-simplex is a tetrahedron. The faces of a k-simplex are simplices formed by subsets of its vertices. Simplices are the building blocks of simplicial complexes and simplicial homology.

contrasts.differential: A simplex is a specific convex polytope; a cell in a CW complex is a copy of D^n attached by any continuous map. Cells are more general
A face is a sub-simplex obtained by deleting vertices; the simplex is the ambient object containing its faces

definition: A face of a k-simplex sigma = [v_0, ..., v_k] is any simplex spanned by a subset of its vertices. The (k-1)-dimensional faces (obtained by omitting one vertex) are called facets or codimension-1 faces. The face relation defines the combinatorial structure of simplicial complexes.

contrasts.differential: The simplex is the ambient object; faces are its sub-simplices. Every face of a simplex in a simplicial complex is also in the complex
The boundary of a simplex (as a topological space) consists of all its proper faces. The boundary operator in homology is the formal alternating sum of face inclusions

definition: In homology theory, the boundary operator d_n: C_n -> C_{n-1} maps n-chains to (n-1)-chains. For a simplex [v_0,...,v_n], d([v_0,...,v_n]) = sum_{i=0}^n (-1)^i [v_0,...,v_i-hat,...,v_n] where v_i-hat means v_i is omitted. The key property is d^2 = 0 (the boundary of a boundary is zero). Topologically, the boundary of a disk is a circle, of a solid ball is a sphere.

contrasts.differential: Boundaries are always cycles (d^2=0), but not all cycles are boundaries. The quotient cycles/boundaries is the homology group
A chain is any formal sum of simplices; a boundary is a chain that is in the image of the boundary operator

definition: In homology, an n-cycle is an n-chain z with dz = 0 (z is in the kernel of the boundary operator). Cycles that are boundaries (z = d(w) for some (n+1)-chain w) are called trivial cycles. The n-th homology group H_n = Z_n/B_n (cycles modulo boundaries) measures the non-trivial cycles. In graph theory, a cycle is a closed path with no repeated vertices.

contrasts.differential: Every boundary is a cycle but not conversely. Non-trivial homology means there exist cycles that are not boundaries
A chain is an arbitrary formal sum of simplices; a cycle is a chain with zero boundary

definition: In simplicial homology, an n-chain is a formal linear combination of oriented n-simplices with coefficients in a ring R (typically Z, Q, or a field). The free abelian group (or R-module) of n-chains is denoted C_n(K; R). Chains form a chain complex connected by boundary operators: ... -> C_{n+1} -> C_n -> C_{n-1} -> ...

contrasts.differential: Chains are formal sums of simplices; cochains are linear functions on chains. Cohomology uses cochains
All n-chains form the chain group C_n; cycles are the subgroup ker(d_n) of chains with zero boundary

definition: A sequence of groups and homomorphisms ... -> A_{n+1} -> A_n -> A_{n-1} -> ... is exact at A_n if im(f_{n+1}) = ker(f_n). The sequence is exact if it is exact at every group. A short exact sequence 0 -> A -> B -> C -> 0 means A injects into B, and C is the quotient B/A. Long exact sequences (e.g., Mayer-Vietoris, long exact sequence of a pair) are fundamental computational tools in algebraic topology.

contrasts.differential: A chain complex only requires d^2 = 0 (im subset of ker); an exact sequence requires im = ker (homology vanishes everywhere)
A short exact sequence has only three nonzero terms; a long exact sequence can have arbitrarily many
